section: Educational Psychology · Ch10 — Memory, Forgetting & Transfer
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A student glances at a phone number, holds it in mind just long enough to dial it, and then forgets it entirely. This describes the limited-capacity, brief store called:
explanation: Short-term/working memory holds a small amount of information briefly (seconds, ~7±2 items) unless rehearsed for transfer to long-term storage. Sensory memory is even briefer (milliseconds), before attention selects information for STM.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch10 — Memory, Forgetting & Transfer
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: Hermann Ebbinghaus's experiments on nonsense syllables showed that forgetting is:

options.option_text: Steepest immediately after learning, then levels off gradually
A constant, uniform rate across all time intervals
Absent entirely if the material was ever meaningful
Faster for meaningful material than for nonsense material

explanation: The Ebbinghaus forgetting curve shows rapid initial memory loss followed by a slower decline — the basis for spaced revision soon after learning. Meaningful material is actually retained better/longer than nonsense syllables.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch10 — Memory, Forgetting & Transfer
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A student who has just learned French vocabulary finds it harder to recall German vocabulary learned earlier. This is best explained by:

options.option_text: Retroactive interference — new learning disrupting recall of older learning
Proactive interference — older learning disrupting new learning

explanation: Retroactive interference occurs when newer learning (French) interferes with recall of earlier learning (German). Proactive interference would be the reverse — old learning disrupting the new.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch10 — Memory, Forgetting & Transfer
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: A student who has mastered riding a bicycle learns to ride a motorbike faster because of shared balancing skills. This is an example of:
explanation: When previous learning facilitates new learning (shared balancing skill helping motorbike riding), it is positive transfer. Negative transfer would occur if old habits actively hindered the new skill (e.g. gear-shift confusion between different vehicles).

section: Educational Psychology · Ch10 — Memory, Forgetting & Transfer
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: Teaching pupils to remember the colours of the rainbow using 'VIBGYOR' is an example of which memory aid?
explanation: VIBGYOR is an acronym — the first letters of Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red form a memorable word. The method of loci uses imagined spatial locations; chunking groups items (like phone numbers) into units.
